hops.afterHeading: The tug of war: where the voltage goes
hops.title: Why Sichuan peppercorns make your lips buzz
hops.text: Chili peppers burn. Sichuan peppercorns also make your lips buzz, though nothing is touching them. The cause is hydroxy-alpha-sanshool, which blocks potassium channels that are open at rest. With potassium's rope pulling more weakly, the voltage drifts up toward threshold. In mice, sanshool makes nearly every D-hair fibre, one kind of very sensitive touch receptor, fire with nothing touching the skin. In 2013, researchers dabbed ground pepper mixed in alcohol onto volunteers' lower lips, then had them compare the tingle with a vibration on a fingertip, over and over. On average the tingle matched a 50-hertz vibration: touch fibres reporting a buzz that was never there.

sources.citation: Bautista, D. M., Sigal, Y. M., Milstein, A. D., Garrison, J. L., Zorn, J. A., Tsuruda, P. R., Nicoll, R. A., & Julius, D., Pungent agents from Szechuan peppers excite sensory neurons by inhibiting two-pore potassium channels, Nature Neuroscience 11:772-779, 2008

Lennertz RC, Tsunozaki M, Bautista DM, Stucky CL, Physiological basis of tingling paresthesia evoked by hydroxy-alpha-sanshool, Journal of Neuroscience 30:4353-4361, 2010

hops.afterHeading: How three gates make one spike
hops.title: The poisonous bird that jams sodium channels open
hops.text: In the late 1980s, graduate student Jack Dumbacher was studying birds of paradise in Papua New Guinea when a hooded pitohui, an orange-and-black songbird caught in his net, scratched his hand. He licked the scratch, and his mouth burned and went numb. The next year he licked one of its feathers on purpose. Same result. The bird's skin and feathers carry homobatrachotoxin, one of a family of toxins also found in poison-dart frogs and in small beetles these birds eat. Batrachotoxins make sodium channels open at lower voltages and disrupt inactivation, so sodium current lingers and the membrane cannot reset for the next spike.

hops.title: Why a stubbed toe often hurts twice
hops.text: Next time you stub your toe, and you will, notice whether it hurts twice. Often a sharp jab comes first, one you can point to exactly. Then a duller, spreading ache arrives and stays. That classic sharp first pain is carried by thin, lightly myelinated fibres at roughly 5 to 30 metres per second. The ache rides bare C fibres at around 1 metre per second. Over the metre or so of nerve from toe to spinal cord, those speeds put the ache's signal about a second behind the jab's. Same toe, same kind of spike, two kinds of axon.

audio.title: Buzzing lips, frog weights and a warm bath
audio.transcript:
Here are three true stories about the spike: one from a dinner table, one from a frog, and one from a warm bath.

Start with dinner. Sichuan pepper can make your lips buzz, as if a phone were vibrating against them, with nothing touching them at all. That tingle is what makes the spice feel so different from a chili. The buzz comes from a compound called hydroxy-alpha-sanshool. In studies of mouse sensory neurons, it blocks potassium channels that are normally open at rest. Remember the tug of war. Potassium's rope usually holds the voltage down near potassium's equilibrium potential. Weaken that rope, and the voltage drifts up toward threshold. In mice, sanshool makes nearly every D-hair fibre, one kind of very sensitive touch receptor, fire with nothing touching the skin. In twenty thirteen, researchers dabbed ground Sichuan pepper, mixed in alcohol, onto volunteers' lower lips. Then, over and over, they asked which felt faster: the tingle on the lip, or a vibration on a fingertip. On average, the tingle matched a vibration of fifty hertz. The mouse recordings tell us how a spice can start a buzz that was never there.

The second story starts with a puzzle that the all-or-none rule creates. A fibre starting from rest fires much the same size spike whether the push is weak or strong. So how can one fibre report how far its muscle has been stretched? In the mid nineteen twenties, Edgar Adrian and Yngve Zotterman worked with a thin muscle from a frog's chest. They trimmed it down, strip by strip, until the record seemed to come from a single stretch receptor on a single nerve fibre. Then they hung tiny weights on the muscle. More stretch never made the spikes any taller. It made them come faster. Adrian later described a discharge that began at about ten spikes a second and reached fifty or more as the stretch increased. A single fibre cannot shout. So it talks faster.

The third story is gentler, and it is about people. In eighteen ninety, the eye doctor Wilhelm Uhthoff noticed something in four out of a hundred of his patients with multiple sclerosis. Their vision got worse when they exercised and came back after they rested. He blamed the exercise. Later researchers worked out that the real trigger was a rise in body temperature. Today, somewhere between sixty and eighty percent of people with M S notice that their symptoms get temporarily worse in the heat. Here is the link to this lesson. A fibre with damaged myelin may have only just enough current to carry a spike past the bare stretch. In the most vulnerable fibres, a small rise in temperature can use up that margin, and the signal does not get through. Doctors once even used a hot bath as a rough test for the disease. The kind news, from the M S Trust, is that these heat flares usually settle within a few hours of cooling down, and they are not usually a sign of new damage.

Turned-down potassium on your lips, faster spikes for a heavier weight, and a warm day that tests a thin margin. One spike, three very different places to meet it.
